field.title: Creativity Techniques
field.description: Controlled vocabulary for creativity-techniques pedagogy in higher-education design studios — foundations, ideation repertoires, development methods, workplace application, technology-mediated practice, personal development, and a critical scholarly layer.

subfields.title: Creativity and Technology
subfields.description: Digital and generative tools as ideation partners, with authorship, originality, and assessment questions for HE design studios.

concepts.definition: Stage-specific use of generative models to propose, vary, or reframe ideas during early ideation while keeping problem framing and final judgment with the human studio team.
Software or model used to expand the search space of concepts—sketch assistants, semantic maps, generative image tools—without substituting for brief analysis or critique.
Using generative image or layout systems to produce rapid visual candidates for discussion, distinct from craft-software training or final production pipelines.
Research and practice concerned with machines producing outputs judged novel and valuable, adjacent to studio pedagogy when tools propose candidate ideas rather than execute fixed rules.
Studio arrangements that allocate roles between learners and models—prompting, curating, critiquing, documenting—so collaboration remains legible to assessment and ethics review.
The question of who counts as author when model outputs are selected, edited, or orchestrated in a design process, central to portfolio, credit, and disclosure norms in HE.
Presentation of AI-assisted or derivative work as wholly novel authorship without process visibility, critiqued in frontier studio discourse as masking weak problem framing.
Documenting prompts, edits, model versions, and human decisions so that creative process can be assessed alongside product under ambient generative assistance.
The ability to formulate constraints, references, and iteration strategies when working with generative tools, treated as studio craft rather than vendor shortcut mastery alone.
Creative work whose tempo, material, and collaboration patterns are shaped by digital platforms and models, requiring pedagogy distinct from analog-only method canons.

subfields.title: Critical Layer
subfields.description: Ideology, labour, and GenAI authorship critiques for debate hours and bibliography ethics in creativity-techniques curricula (Media Prospector units C1–C3).

concepts.definition: Institutional presentation of creativity as a generic employability checkbox detached from technique repertoires, critique, and material conditions of design work in higher education.
Cultural and managerial narratives that treat creativity as innate spark or innovation fuel, obscuring labour, method, power, and pedagogy in design studios.
Critical claim that normative assessment, ranking, and conformity in education can inhibit exploratory thinking unless studios explicitly protect divergent phases and reflective review.
Scholarly and studio critique of design thinking as managerial product or innovation theatre divorced from situated design practice and ethical judgment.
The often-invisible work of ideation, mood boards, iteration, and emotional labour in design professions, including unpaid or under-credited phases of creative production.
Speculative creative labour—competitions, pitches, internships—performed before contract or payment, raising questions about exploitation in professional entry paths.
Normalisation of constant productivity and self-branding as signs of creative worth, critiqued for eroding reflection, collaboration, and sustainable practice in design careers.
Overconfidence in unstructured group brainstorming as optimal ideation despite documented issues with evaluation apprehension, dominance, and production blocking.
How teams and firms assign ownership of ideas, presentation, and execution, a power-laden process especially salient in student group work and client-facing studios.
Norms for disclosure, consent, and fair credit when generative tools contribute to ideation or production in academic and professional design settings.
Maintaining fair evaluation of student creative process and product when ambient generative assistance can produce polished outputs with minimal visible effort.
Expectation that learners document tool use, prompts, and edits so reviewers can distinguish human judgment from model output in portfolios and exams.
Critical analysis of performances of novelty—human or AI-assisted—that conceal derivation, weak framing, or labour conditions behind surface innovation.
Critical attention to gender, class, disability, and colonial histories that shape which creators and methods are centred or erased in creativity pedagogy and industry canons.

subfields.title: Foundations and Importance
subfields.description: Definitions, process models, and pedagogical rationales for teaching creativity as method under professional constraint in design higher education.

concepts.definition: The studio pacing principle of separating open idea production from disciplined selection and refinement, downstream of mid-century divergent-thinking research and still used to structure briefs in design schools.
A widely used definitional pair treating creative outcomes as both new relative to a context and fit for a stated problem, audience, or brief constraint.
Rhodes's framework locating creativity in person, process, product, and press (environment), used in design pedagogy to avoid reducing creativity to individual talent or single artifacts alone.
Kaufman and Beghetto's distinction among mini-c, little-c, Pro-c, and Big-C creative accomplishment, helping HE studios calibrate expectations from classroom exercises to professional practice.
The pedagogical claim that creative performance in design can be developed through structured methods, rehearsal, and critique rather than treated as an unexplained gift.
The belief that creativity is an innate trait possessed by a fixed minority, critiqued in studio discourse because it obscures method, practice conditions, and equitable access to creative education.
An indeterminate design problem whose framing, stakeholders, and success criteria remain contested, requiring iterative reframing rather than a single correct solution.
A contested field of talk spanning situated design practice, commercial method kits, and managerial innovation rhetoric; taught critically in HE studios as discourse, not as neutral procedure.

Studio pedagogy modeled on Schön's reflection-in-action, in which designers learn by conversing with the situation through sketching, prototyping, and critique rather than executing a fixed algorithm.
An integrative competency target in design HE combining analytic judgment, generative exploration, and metacognitive review of one's own process under brief constraints.
Higher-education design teaching organized around project briefs, desk crits, peer review, and iterative making, treating the studio as a semi-professional learning environment.

subfields.title: Idea Development and Solutions
subfields.description: Methods for turning selected ideas into workable design solutions under analytical, user-centred, and sprint-class development stacks.

concepts.definition: The studio phase in which a shortlisted concept is elaborated through sketches, models, scenarios, and tests until it meets brief constraints and can be defended to peers or stakeholders.
A structured development lineage—problem finding, idea finding, solution finding, acceptance finding—used in design pedagogy to connect ideation with implementation and stakeholder buy-in.

A time-compressed development stack combining problem framing, sketching, decision, prototyping, and user testing, taught as a workplace-ready method while distinguished from peer-reviewed studio pedagogy proof.
Breaking a selected idea or wicked problem into sub-problems, functions, or constraints so that development can proceed systematically rather than by aesthetic guesswork alone.
Using sketch, diagram, storyboard, or napkin-class visual notation to make problem structure, stakeholders, and assumptions visible before committing to a solution direction.
Treating quick drawing not as presentation polish but as a cognitive tool for exploring form, sequence, and interaction during solution development.
Building low- to mid-fidelity artifacts—paper, foam, clickable flows, coded stubs—to test a solution hypothesis before full production commitment.
A solution lens that iterates development against observed or inferred user needs, contexts, and pain points, common in design-thinking method stacks taught with critical awareness of simplification.
Designerly inference that proposes plausible solutions under incomplete information, associated with design cognition research and distinct from purely deductive or inductive problem solving.
The set of feasible design responses bounded by brief, materials, time, and stakeholder constraints; studio teaching makes this space explorable rather than treating the first idea as inevitable.

subfields.title: Idea Generation and Selection
subfields.description: Graphic, semantic, multifocal, and group methods for producing ideas under brief and selecting candidates for development.

concepts.definition: Visual prompts—images, diagrams, collage fragments, or constrained drawing tasks—used to trigger associations and divergent responses before verbal refinement in studio ideation.
A method linking words, concepts, or domains through metaphor, analogy, or lexical chains to escape literal brief readings and widen the idea search space.
Deliberate inspection of a problem from multiple viewpoints, scales, or user positions so that a brief is not solved from a single habitual frame.
Production of many varied candidate ideas in response to an open prompt, prior to convergent filtering against brief criteria.
Filtering, ranking, or combining generated ideas using explicit criteria such as feasibility, fit to brief, originality, and stakeholder value.
Guilford-derived dimensions still used in studio rubrics to describe divergent output quantity, categorical variety, and novelty relative to peers or prior solutions.
Deliberate departure from established problem paths through provocation, reversal, or oblique moves, associated with de Bono and widely rehearsed in group studio exercises.

A role-separated group ideation protocol assigning emotional and functional stances (facts, risks, benefits, creativity, process, synthesis) to reduce premature convergence and dominance in critique sessions.

A facilitated group ideation format emphasizing deferred judgment and quantity of ideas, descended from Osborn's applied-imagination lineage and taught with caveats about documented group-process limits.
A deck of constraint and prompt cards used to interrupt habitual thinking during studio blocks, associated with Eno and Schmidt and reusable as low-tech ideation infrastructure.
The deliberate craft of generating candidate concepts at volume and variety, distinct from later development into workable solutions or polished deliverables.
A time-boxed studio block structured for divergent production and initial convergent selection, often combining individual sketching with group review under a brief.

subfields.title: Personal Development
subfields.description: Creative confidence, mental blocks, reflective and interpersonal skills, and group dynamics as conditions for sustained creative practice in design HE.

concepts.definition: A learner's willingness to propose, test, and defend ideas under uncertainty, developed through structured method rehearsal and safe-to-fail studio iteration rather than motivational slogans alone.

A perceived inability to generate or move forward on ideas despite available time and resources, addressed in studio through constraint exercises, role play, and environmental change rather than willpower alone.
Deliberate techniques—oblique prompts, reframing, physical movement, switching media—to restore productive exploration when a learner stalls on a brief.
Patterns of participation, dominance, and support in team ideation that affect whose ideas survive selection and how credit is distributed in studio projects.
The skill of identifying and mobilising complementary strengths within a design team during cooperative studio projects.
Adjusting one's facilitative or directive stance in a creative team according to task phase, expertise gaps, and deadline pressure rather than fixed personality roles.
Combining self-review of one's creative process with respectful feedback to peers, linking Schön-style reflection to communication competencies in design HE.
The capacity to self-direct exploration and decision-making within explicit project constraints, a learning outcome distinct from unconstrained self-expression.
Habits—reflection, collaboration, method rotation—that help designers continue producing under repetition, rejection, and professional pressure beyond a single course.

subfields.title: Workplace Application
subfields.description: Applying creativity techniques under client briefs, deadlines, competition, and professional ethics in design practice.

concepts.definition: A formal or informal specification of goals, constraints, audience, and deliverables against which creative methods must produce accountable outcomes in professional design work.
Structured conversations, tests, or reviews with clients, users, or internal decision-makers to check that a developing solution remains aligned with needs and feasibility before commitment.
Non-negotiable limits—budget, brand guidelines, regulation, production capacity— that shape which creative moves are viable in workplace settings as opposed to open classroom exercises.

Organisational language that positions design creativity as driver of new products, services, or processes; taught critically alongside method repertoires because framing affects credit, risk, and resource allocation.
Contexts in which creative methods support new workflows, teams, or offerings inside firms or institutions, linking studio technique to change-management situations.
Choosing among creative alternatives with explicit justification—evidence, trade-offs, ethics—rather than charisma or hierarchy alone, a core professional competency in design leadership.
Evaluating creative proposals for harm, exclusion, misrepresentation, or labour exploitation before they ship, treated as part of professional design practice rather than an optional add-on.
The communicative work—shared language, documentation, critique norms—that lets groups coordinate creative output under deadline without losing traceability of decisions.
Workplace conditions in which creative methods must deliver under time boxes, pitches, or market windows, changing which techniques are appropriate and how originality is evaluated.
A structured presentation of creative direction, rationale, and prototypes to secure client or internal approval, linking ideation repertoires to professional persuasion and documentation.
